title: What is the difference between the Factory and Abstract Factory patterns?
shortTitle: What is the difference between the Factory and Abstract Factory patterns

s1_definition.profdef: The Factory (or Factory Method) pattern creates a single product from one hierarchy, choosing the concrete class behind a method. The Abstract Factory pattern creates families of related products that are designed to be used together, through a factory interface whose implementations each produce one complete, consistent family. In short, a Factory decides one product; an Abstract Factory decides a matching set of products and guarantees they belong together.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the Factory is the single counter that hands Rajesh the one thing he asked for, such as a savings-account kit. The Abstract Factory is the regional branch office that hands him a whole matched set for his region — the regional form, the regional card design, and the regional cheque book — all guaranteed to belong to the same region so nothing clashes. One gives you a single item; the other gives you a consistent bundle.
s1_definition.oneliner: Factory produces one product; Abstract Factory produces a whole matching family of products through a factory of factories.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Factory (or Factory Method) pattern creates a single product from one hierarchy, choosing the concrete class behind a method. The Abstract Factory pattern creates families of related products that are designed to be used together, through a factory interface whose implementations each produce one complete, consistent family. In short, a Factory decides one product; an Abstract Factory decides a matching set of products and guarantees they belong together.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the Factory is the single counter that hands Rajesh the one thing he asked for, such as a savings-account kit. The Abstract Factory is the regional branch office that hands him a whole matched set for his region — the regional form, the regional card design, and the regional cheque book — all guaranteed to belong to the same region so nothing clashes. One gives you a single item; the other gives you a consistent bundle.

**One line to remember:** Factory produces one product; Abstract Factory produces a whole matching family of products through a factory of factories.

sections.s2_technical:
The Factory pattern has one product interface and one factory method that returns one product. For example `PaymentProcessor p = ProcessorFactory.create(PaymentType.UPI)` returns a single UPI processor. The decision is "which one concrete class," and the output is one object. Adding a new product means adding a class and one branch or registry entry.

The Abstract Factory pattern has multiple product interfaces that are related, and a factory interface with a method per product. Each concrete factory produces a complete, consistent family. For example a `BankingUiFactory` might declare `Button createButton()` and `Statement createStatement()`, and a `RetailUiFactory` returns a RetailButton and a RetailStatement while a `CorporateUiFactory` returns a CorporateButton and a CorporateStatement. The guarantee is that you never mix a retail button with a corporate statement, because one factory produces the whole set.

The structural difference is the number of products. Factory answers one question: which concrete product. Abstract Factory answers a bigger question: which family of concrete products, where the family members must be consistent with each other. An Abstract Factory is often described as a factory of factories, because each method inside it is essentially its own factory method for one product in the family.

The dependency difference matters. With a Factory, the client depends on one product interface and the factory. With an Abstract Factory, the client depends only on the abstract factory interface and the abstract product interfaces, never on any concrete product or concrete factory. This lets you swap the entire family by swapping the single factory instance the client was given.

When to use which: use a Factory when you have one product type whose concrete class varies, such as choosing a settlement handler by trade type. Use an Abstract Factory when you have several products that must vary together as a consistent set, such as building a report with a matching header, body formatter, and footer, or rendering a UI theme where all widgets must match.

A code example showing the Abstract Factory contract: `ReportFamilyFactory f = new RegulatoryFamilyFactory(); Header h = f.createHeader(); Formatter fm = f.createFormatter();` — here h and fm are guaranteed to be regulatory, and swapping to `new CustomerFamilyFactory()` swaps both at once.

A senior nuance: an Abstract Factory is more machinery than a plain Factory, so you should only reach for it when the consistency of a family genuinely matters. If the products do not need to match, a set of independent factory methods is simpler. Overusing Abstract Factory adds interfaces and indirection for no benefit.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India generates two very different kinds of documents, and the pieces of each must be consistent.

Problem 1 — Picking one settlement handler (Factory). When a trade arrives, the system needs the one correct settlement handler for its type. This is a single-product decision, so a plain Factory is enough.

Problem 2 — Building a consistent document family (Abstract Factory). A regulatory filing must have a regulatory header, a regulatory number formatter that renders amounts in the regulator's required style, and a regulatory footer with legal text. A customer statement must have a friendly header, a customer-style formatter, and a marketing footer. If a developer accidentally combined a regulatory header with a customer formatter, the document would be invalid. The three pieces must always come from the same family, which is exactly what Abstract Factory guarantees.

Problem 3 — Swapping the whole family at once. The reporting code should be able to switch from regulatory to customer documents by changing only which factory it was handed, without touching the generation logic. This is the core Abstract Factory benefit.

The demo first shows a simple Factory producing one settlement handler, then an Abstract Factory producing a complete, matching document family for Rajesh's account statement, proving that header, formatter, and footer always belong together.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a request for an equity settlement handler, then a statement for Rajesh's account SAV2001 with balance Rs.949,950, rendered first as a regulatory document and then as a customer document.

Step 1: SettlementFactory.create(EQUITY) runs. This plain Factory returns one product, an EquitySettlement, as a SettlementStrategy. The decision was a single-product decision.

Step 2: A RegulatoryFactory is created and handed to renderStatement. The client code holds only a DocumentFactory reference, so it does not know whether it is regulatory or customer.

Step 3: renderStatement calls createHeader, createFormatter, and createFooter on the factory. Because this is the RegulatoryFactory, all three products come from the regulatory family: a RegulatoryHeader, a RegulatoryFormatter, and a RegulatoryFooter. They are guaranteed consistent because one factory produced the whole set.

Step 4: The formatter renders the balance in the regulatory style, INR 949950.00, the header shows the RBI filing title, and the footer shows the regulatory legal text. The document is internally consistent.

Step 5: Now a CustomerFactory is created and handed to the exact same renderStatement method. Only the factory instance changed; the rendering logic is identical.

Step 6: This time createHeader, createFormatter, and createFooter return the customer family: a friendly header, a Rs. style formatter, and a thank-you footer. The whole family switched together by swapping one object.

Step 7: Comparing the two outputs shows the key point. With Abstract Factory the three pieces always match, and switching families is a one-line change, which a plain Factory could not guarantee because it only produces one product at a time.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Factory → single product: EquitySettlement
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] RBI REGULATORY FILING | SAV2001 balance=INR 949950.00 | Filed per RBI circular 2024-X
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Your Account Statement | SAV2001 balance=Rs.949950 | Thank you for banking with us!
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  FACTORY (one product)
    create(EQUITY) → EquitySettlement
    │ single object, single decision
    ▼

  ABSTRACT FACTORY (one matching family)
    renderStatement(RegulatoryFactory, ...)
      │ createHeader()    → RegulatoryHeader   ┐
      │ createFormatter() → RegulatoryFormatter├ all REGULATORY
      │ createFooter()    → RegulatoryFooter   ┘
      ▼ "RBI FILING | INR 949950.00 | Filed per RBI..."

    renderStatement(CustomerFactory, ...)   ← swap ONE factory
      │ createHeader()    → CustomerHeader    ┐
      │ createFormatter() → CustomerFormatter ├ all CUSTOMER
      │ createFooter()    → CustomerFooter    ┘
      ▼ "Your Statement | Rs.949950 | Thank you..."

  Guarantee: pieces NEVER mixed across families
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Factory vs Abstract Factory ═══

  ┌─ Key difference ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Factory:          one product interface → one product      │
  │ Abstract Factory: factory interface → a FAMILY of products │
  │   (a "factory of factories", guarantees consistency)       │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ When to use ──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Factory: concrete type of ONE product varies               │
  │ Abstract Factory: several products must vary TOGETHER      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  Factory:
    SettlementFactory ──create()──▶ SettlementStrategy ┤▷ EquitySettlement

  Abstract Factory:
    ┌──────────────────────┐
    │ <<interface>>        │
    │ DocumentFactory      │
    │ + createHeader()     │
    │ + createFormatter()  │
    │ + createFooter()     │
    └─────────┬────────────┘
       implements
      ┌────────┴─────────┐
      ▼                  ▼
  RegulatoryFactory   CustomerFactory
      │ produce           │ produce
      ▼                   ▼
  {RegHeader,          {CustHeader,
   RegFormatter,        CustFormatter,
   RegFooter}           CustFooter}

  ── Call Chain (Abstract Factory) ─────────────────────────────
  1. factory = new RegulatoryFactory()
  2. renderStatement(factory, acct, balance)
  3.   factory.createHeader()    → RegulatoryHeader
  4.   factory.createFormatter() → RegulatoryFormatter
  5.   factory.createFooter()    → RegulatoryFooter
  6. swap to CustomerFactory → whole family changes, logic unchanged
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The difference comes down to how many products the pattern creates and whether they must be consistent with each other. The Factory, or Factory Method, pattern creates a single product from one hierarchy; it hides the new keyword behind a method and decides which one concrete class to instantiate. The Abstract Factory pattern creates a whole family of related products that are designed to be used together, through a factory interface whose implementations each produce one complete, consistent family. People often describe the Abstract Factory as a factory of factories, because each method inside it is like its own factory method for one member of the family.

The practical way I explain it is with my work at the National Bank of India. When a trade arrives and I need the one correct settlement handler for its type, that is a single-product decision, so a plain Factory is enough. But when I generate documents, a regulatory filing needs a regulatory header, a regulatory amount formatter, and a regulatory footer, while a customer statement needs a friendly header, a customer-style formatter, and a marketing footer. The three pieces must always come from the same family, because combining a regulatory header with a customer formatter would produce an invalid document. That consistency requirement is exactly why I reach for an Abstract Factory.

The big benefit of the Abstract Factory is that the client depends only on the abstract factory interface and the abstract product interfaces, never on any concrete product. So my report-generation code takes a DocumentFactory and calls createHeader, createFormatter, and createFooter, and it has no idea whether it is building a regulatory or a customer document. Switching the entire family is a one-line change, I just hand it a different factory, and all three products switch together while the generation logic stays untouched.

The senior judgment I add is that an Abstract Factory is more machinery than a plain Factory, with more interfaces and indirection, so I only use it when the consistency of a family genuinely matters. If the products do not need to match each other, a plain Factory or a couple of independent factory methods is simpler and clearer. Knowing when the extra structure pays for itself, rather than applying it everywhere, is the real signal of understanding both patterns.

---

keyPoints: Singleton: one instance globally — eager, lazy, enum
Factory: encapsulate object creation — decouple client from concrete class
Builder: step-by-step construction — complex objects with many optional fields
Prototype: clone existing object — avoid expensive construction
